cultivar: Yunnan large-leaf (for Dian Hong broken grades)
processing: Withered, then broken by a traditional roller, a Rotorvane or a CTC machine, then oxidised and dried; CTC lots come out as small granules. Sieving sorts the tea into size grades.
harvest_season: Machine-made over a long season; in Yunnan the picking runs from mid-March to mid-November across spring, summer and autumn.
appearance_dry: Small even particles or granules, dark with a reddish shine.
appearance_liquor: Deep, bright red, darker than whole-leaf black tea from the same area.
appearance_wet: Fine coppery fragments with no whole leaf to see.
taste_profile: Strong and brisk, as with other broken black teas: quick, full colour and a firm malty grip that stands up to milk and sugar.

brewing.notes: Normally brewed Western-style or in a bag. Small particles extract fast, so keep it to two or three minutes, or add milk if it goes long.

vintage_note: Typically sold by size grade rather than by vintage. As with other broken teas, there is no reason to age it; drink it within a year or two, while it still has its briskness.
description:
Hong sui cha simply means broken black tea, the Chinese name for the small-particle grades that fill most of the world's tea bags. It is made in China too, though its best-known home is elsewhere, and in Yunnan it is the second face of Dian Hong beside the whole-leaf gongfu.

The breaking is the point. Chinese usage covers several methods: traditional rollers, whose output is lower but richer in taste, and machine routes, including rotorvane, LTP and CTC. Smaller pieces oxidise evenly and brew fast.

The cup is dark, strong and quick. Do not gongfu it: a couple of minutes in a mug is enough, and more just adds bitterness. It is made for milk, sugar or blending as much as for drinking plain.

Broken does not mean bad here, but look for an even particle and a fresh smell.
history:
Chinese terminology splits broken black tea by method: traditional, and non-traditional, the latter covering rotor (Rotorvane), CTC and LTP machine-made teas. The machine methods are also used internationally.

In China the style has a place in Yunnan, where Dian Hong divides into gongfu and broken tea, and in Guangxi, which has its own CTC processing standard. Its history here is more industrial than storied, with little in the way of a single founder or origin account.
